video_title: The Asset That Could Be the Market’s Biggest Mispricing
gist: David Ivan, co-CIO of Kernick Global Investors ($10B+ AUM), argues investors chronically underprice scarcity in commodities (gold, platinum, copper, farmland) while overpaying for cap-weighted, US-heavy, AI-driven indices; he lays out a value framework of buying more as assets get cheaper relative to appraised worth, and walks through specific country and sector opportunities (Korea, Kazakhstan, China's CGN, Brazil, Philippines, Indonesia).

insights.claim: Since the guest's birth, the money supply has risen roughly 111x and total debt roughly 135x, meaning the US dollar has lost more than 99% of its purchasing power over that period.
insights.speaker: David Ivan, co-CIO, Kernick Global Investors
insights.so_what: Frames the multi-decade case for owning scarce, unprintable assets (gold, oil, copper, farmland) as a hedge against currency debasement.
insights.quote: I.e. the dollar's lost more than 99% of its value.

insights.claim: Despite decades of monetary debasement, commodities like oil, gold, and copper still make up only a low single-digit percentage of major equity indexes, down from roughly half the index decades ago, showing investors still underappreciate scarcity.
insights.speaker: David Ivan, co-CIO, Kernick Global Investors
insights.so_what: Suggests structural underweighting of real assets in benchmark portfolios remains a persistent, exploitable mispricing rather than a fad that has already played out.

insights.claim: Commodity investors are unique in assuming the price of the underlying resource (oil, gold, copper) declines every year in discounted cash flow models even as the dollar itself is assumed to lose value, whereas every other industry assumes the dollar depreciates over time — a double standard that makes longer-life reserves get valued cheaper than they should.
insights.speaker: David Ivan, co-CIO, Kernick Global Investors
insights.so_what: Explains a specific analytical error the market makes when pricing resource companies, which value investors can exploit by owning long-reserve-life miners and producers.

insights.claim: Platinum trades at a discount to gold (around $1,800 vs. needing roughly $2,500 to incentivize new mine construction) even though platinum has historically carried a scarcity premium over gold, making it a specific mispriced commodity opportunity as of the interview.
insights.speaker: David Ivan, co-CIO, Kernick Global Investors
insights.so_what: A concrete, checkable price level ($2,500 incentive price vs. ~$1,800 spot) investors can track as a signal for when new platinum supply gets built or the price re-rates.
insights.quote: at the time I was there, platinum needed to more than triple to catch up to gold

insights.claim: Natural gas prices in the US and Canada are seen as too low to sustain the supply growth needed for demand, and nickel prices likely need to rise further to fund the mining investment required for battery demand.
insights.speaker: David Ivan, co-CIO, Kernick Global Investors
insights.so_what: Flags natural gas and nickel as commodities where current prices may be below the incentive price needed to sustain future supply, implying upside risk to prices.

insights.claim: The fund has cut its gold position by roughly two-thirds from a prior weighting of over 20% of the portfolio, rotating that capital into platinum, copper, and other commodities that are now more mispriced than gold.
insights.speaker: David Ivan, co-CIO, Kernick Global Investors
insights.so_what: Signals that within the resource complex, capital is actively rotating away from gold (which has already re-rated) toward platinum and copper as the next mispriced scarce assets.

insights.claim: Citing the 18th-century economist Richard Cantillon, the guest argues money printing is inflationary but not neutral: those closest to newly created money get richer first, while hard assets like metals, energy, food, and farmland only catch up to the inflation later, creating a lag investors can exploit.
insights.speaker: David Ivan, co-CIO, Kernick Global Investors
insights.so_what: Provides a macro rationale for holding farmland and metals as a bet on delayed inflation pass-through, with the fund structured so it still profits from cheap valuations even if that macro thesis is wrong.
insights.quote: money sure it's inflationary but it's not neutral

insights.claim: Public farmland-linked companies in Ukraine trade at an 80-90% discount on an enterprise-value-per-hectare basis compared to equivalent farmland in the US Midwest, despite Ukraine having some of the best farmland in the world.
insights.speaker: David Ivan, co-CIO, Kernick Global Investors
insights.so_what: Identifies a specific, quantifiable discount (80-90% per hectare) in publicly traded Ukrainian farmland exposure as a deep-value, high-optionality holding.

themes.theme: Global Value Framework and Asymmetric Position Sizing

insights.claim: The US now makes up roughly two-thirds of global equity market value while representing only about one-fifth or less of the global economy, a valuation gap the guest believes history will eventually correct.
insights.speaker: David Ivan, co-CIO, Kernick Global Investors
insights.so_what: Directly challenges the consensus 'must own the US' allocation stance, implying non-US equities are structurally underweighted relative to their share of global GDP.
insights.quote: Does one fifth or less of the economy deserve to trade at 65% of the market?

insights.claim: The fund's process is explicitly anti-momentum: if a stock appraised as worth 50 and risk-adjusted to 30 trades down to 15, they buy more (upside doubles to 100%) rather than selling, and they trim positions as prices rise toward appraised value rather than riding winners further.
insights.speaker: David Ivan, co-CIO, Kernick Global Investors
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete, replicable position-sizing rule (size up as the price/value gap widens, trim as it closes) that investors can apply instead of momentum-following.

insights.claim: Investors tend to treat all emerging markets as equally risky (a Korean phone company judged as risky as a Zimbabwean chemical company), when in reality emerging markets contain many stable, low-risk businesses like utilities, telecoms, and railroads that are simply mispriced due to this binary perception.
insights.speaker: David Ivan, co-CIO, Kernick Global Investors
insights.so_what: Suggests EM-averse allocators are conflating country risk with business risk, leaving safe, cash-generative EM businesses undervalued relative to developed-market peers.

insights.claim: Because 'you can't do better than the market if you look like the market,' the times to most avoid owning cap-weighted index constituents are precisely when concentration is most extreme — cited as 1929, 1972-73, and the guest's view of the present (2026).
insights.speaker: David Ivan, co-CIO, Kernick Global Investors
insights.so_what: Argues that today's narrow, concentrated index leadership is itself a signal to underweight the largest index names and own out-of-index assets instead.
insights.quote: you can't do better than the market if you look like the market

insights.claim: When Korea's president attempted to seize control of the government and the military intervened to preserve democracy, the Korean stock market fell 25% and the fund increased its Korea allocation to about 19% of the portfolio during the sell-off, buying Hyundai and LG at roughly a third of book value.
insights.speaker: David Ivan, co-CIO, Kernick Global Investors
insights.so_what: A concrete case study of buying into political-crisis-driven panic selling when the underlying business value (book value, competitive position) was unaffected by the news.

insights.claim: After the political shock, the Korean market fully reversed its 25% drop and the fund's Korean holdings were up about a third; since then Korea has rallied further, driven substantially by Samsung and SK Hynix (transcribed as 'Highix'), which the fund does not own, while many other Korean companies still trade below book value.
insights.speaker: David Ivan, co-CIO, Kernick Global Investors
insights.so_what: Flags that Korea's index-level rally is now concentrated in two semiconductor names, so investors chasing 'Korea' broadly may be missing that many non-chip Korean equities remain cheap.

themes.theme: AI Bubble Parallels to Market History

insights.claim: The guest sees today's market (2026) as most closely resembling the end of 1972 into 1973: an extreme market high coinciding with rising inflation, out-of-control fiscal policy and money supply growth, global geopolitical conflict, and a handful of very expensive stocks dominating the index — the setup that preceded the Nifty Fifty collapse.
insights.speaker: David Ivan, co-CIO, Kernick Global Investors
insights.so_what: A specific historical analog investors can use to gauge downside risk: the Nifty Fifty era saw certain 'right in the long run' stocks lose 75-90% of their value over the following years despite ultimately being correct picks.

insights.claim: Every transformative technology in history — canals, railroads, telecom, semiconductors, the internet — became a real, lasting technology and also a financial bubble, because bubbles form specifically around genuine breakthroughs, not around things people know are worthless; AI being real does not mean current AI valuations are justified.
insights.speaker: David Ivan, co-CIO, Kernick Global Investors
insights.so_what: A reusable mental model for separating 'is the technology real' from 'is the current price of the technology's stocks reasonable' — directly applicable to today's AI infrastructure names.
insights.quote: every one of them was a bubble because bubbles always happen around the real deal

insights.claim: The guest argues investors are confusing exciting businesses with good investments, questioning whether AI companies valued at $1-5 trillion that are years away from profitability (if ever) can justify such enormous market caps, given how large the denominator (future profit) would need to become to support them.
insights.speaker: David Ivan, co-CIO, Kernick Global Investors
insights.so_what: A valuation-discipline warning against buying mega-cap AI names purely on narrative, since the earnings growth required to justify $1-5 trillion valuations is extreme.
insights.quote: I think people confuse exciting businesses with good investments.

insights.claim: Energy and materials now make up close to zero (sub-5%) of major US equity indexes versus roughly 30% four to five decades ago, meaning investors no longer get an implicit inflation/energy hedge from simply holding the index and must make an explicit allocation to natural resources to get that exposure.
insights.speaker: David Ivan, co-CIO, Kernick Global Investors
insights.so_what: Explains why passive index investors today are structurally under-hedged against inflation compared to prior cycles, strengthening the case for a standalone natural-resources allocation.

insights.claim: The fund previously held a large position in a dominant Kazakh bank (referred to in the transcript as 'Hick Bank') for its market-share dominance, strong balance sheet, and exposure to an undercapitalized, growing economy, but has since sold most of the position after a substantial run-up in price.
insights.speaker: David Ivan, co-CIO, Kernick Global Investors
insights.so_what: Illustrates the fund's full cycle of buying a mispriced frontier-market bank and exiting after the value gap closed, rather than holding indefinitely.

insights.claim: The fund bought shares of CGN, one of the world's largest nuclear power operators, in China at a steep discount, effectively acquiring newly built nuclear reactors for far less than it costs most of the world to construct new nuclear capacity, framing it as buying a specific undervalued company rather than a bet on China broadly.
insights.speaker: David Ivan, co-CIO, Kernick Global Investors
insights.so_what: A concrete example of using country discounts (demanding extra margin of safety for China-specific risk) to buy nuclear power capacity — relevant given nuclear's role in meeting rising AI-driven electricity demand.
insights.quote: We were able to buy brand new nuclear reactors for uh way cheaper than it takes most of the world to build nuclear reactors.

insights.claim: In the Philippines the fund owns the local equivalent of Costco, and in Indonesia it holds resource-related and food companies, viewing both markets as beaten-down but containing good businesses trading too cheap.
insights.speaker: David Ivan, co-CIO, Kernick Global Investors
insights.so_what: Names specific frontier-market sector exposures (retail-club format in the Philippines, resources/food in Indonesia) investors could research directly.

insights.claim: After spending two months in Brazil doing research, the guest could not find a single person who was bullish on the Brazilian stock market, even though Brazilian real interest rates (12-14%) are far above US rates (around 4%) against similar inflation, which he sees as a contrarian setup where a currency rebound could make Brazilian equities, not fixed income, the place to be.
insights.speaker: David Ivan, co-CIO, Kernick Global Investors
insights.so_what: A textbook contrarian sentiment signal (zero bulls found) combined with a rates argument for why Brazilian equities may be more attractive than the locally popular high-yield bond trade.
insights.quote: Two months in Brazil, the number of people I met that were bullish on their stock market, zero.

themes.theme: AI as a Tool, Not a Replacement for Judgment

insights.claim: The fund tells its analysts their jobs are not at risk from AI as long as they use it correctly: AI should handle shallow analysis while humans retain the deeper, second- and third-level thinking (referencing Howard Marks' concept) needed to form investment judgments, since AI itself cannot think.
insights.speaker: David Ivan, co-CIO, Kernick Global Investors
insights.so_what: Offers a practical division of labor for investment teams adopting AI tools: delegate data-gathering and shallow write-ups, but never delegate the core judgment or thesis formation.
insights.quote: These are wonderful tools. I think they need to be our servant and never our master.

insights.claim: An investor named Peter Kaufman demonstrated that AI, when prompted to write a bull case on Costco from Charlie Munger's perspective versus from Warren Buffett's perspective, produced two different but equally persuasive and excellent reports, illustrating that AI-generated analysis is persuasive regardless of the actual merits of the underlying thesis.
insights.speaker: David Ivan, co-CIO, Kernick Global Investors
insights.so_what: A warning that AI-written investment research can sound compelling on either side of an argument, so investors must supply the judgment and only use AI to write up conclusions already reached, not to form them.
